newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin vows to isolate French judges from politics.
newsitem.headline: Jospin vows to isolate French judges from politics.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin pledged on Thursday to isolate the justice system from politicians to shield investigating magistrates from interference in the conduct of sleaze probes.

"I announce solemnly that from today, no instructions will be given by the justice minister that might affect the pursuit of an individual investigation," he said in a keynote policy address to the National Assembly.
Jospin said the appointment process for investigating magistrates would be reformed to assure that only candidates approved by the Higher Magistrates Council (CSM) be named.
He also pledged a constitutional amendment setting the aim of parity betwen men and women in French public life.
"An independent justice system and respect for the law are fundamental to the republic and to democracy," Jospin said. "Justice must be independent and impartial."
Isolating France's justice system from political influence was a key Socialist promise during the parliamentary election campaign.
The previous centre-right government came under widespread criticism for appearing to meddle in sensitive probes with political overtones.

Outgoing Gaullist minister Jacques Toubon, who lost his seat in the June 1 parliamentary election, had been accused by the media and the then-opposition Socialists of derailing sleaze probes targeting fellow rightists.

In one incident, his ministry chartered a helicopter in Nepal last year to try to find a state prosecutor trekking in the mountains in an unsuccessful attempt to head off an inquiry into Gaullist Paris mayor Jean Tiberi.
Gaullist President Jacques Chirac had also come under fire for naming senior judges with political backgrounds.
New Socialist Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou said on taking over the justice portfolio this month that her top priority would be to restore confidence in the system and ensure its independence.

A panel named by Chirac in January and headed by Supreme Court president Pierre Truche is to report by July 15 on ways of guaranteeing judicial independence, ensuring the legitimacy of the justice system and upholding the presumption of innocence.
But Jospin said he did not want to wait that long before taking the first steps towards shoring up the system's independence.
